LLMs for mobile engineers, from tokens to your app · Puzzle 6 · 7 of 8

Your key is not a secret

The quickest way to ship an AI feature is to put the provider's key in the app and call the model directly. A week later the bill is ten times your users' usage. Here's why a key inside an APK isn't hidden, and the small backend that fixes it.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 2: Your first call

    A call to a model is one HTTP POST: a model name, max_tokens (the most it may write), and messages, a list of turns each marked user or assistant. The response holds the continuation, a stop_reason (end_turn when it finished, max_tokens when it was cut off), and usage: the input and output tokens you pay for. Output tokens cost more than input ones, and each one takes time to generate.

  • Puzzle 3: Why answers stream

    Because the model writes one token at a time, the API can stream: send each piece as it's generated, over one open HTTP response, as server-sent events. Time to first token, not total time, is what makes an app feel fast. On mobile, the stream is a long-lived request: keep it on a background coroutine, append to UI state as events arrive, and cancel it when the user leaves.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 4 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

You put the model provider's key in BuildConfig, obfuscated with R8, Android's build tool that shrinks code and renames it, and call the API straight from the app. It works. Then your usage dashboard shows calls your app never made, around the clock, with prompts that have nothing to do with your feature. How did anyone get the key?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

An API key is a password for your account: whoever sends it, gets served, and you get billed. And an APK is a file anyone can download and unpack. Strings in it can be found; obfuscation, scrambling names to make code harder to read, renames code but a key is still a string the app must send; and even if you hide it well, the key travels in every request from a phone the attacker controls, where they can intercept their own traffic. Google Cloud's guidance is plain: don't include API keys in client code.

So the key lives on a server you control, a proxy backend:

  1. The app calls your server, sending the user's login token: the token your app receives when the user signs in, which proves to your server who they are.
  2. Your server checks who it is, applies limits per user ("20 requests a day on the free plan"), and builds the request: your system prompt, the user's message.
  3. Your server adds the API key and calls the model, streaming the answer back to the app (puzzle 3).

The key never leaves the server. If one user abuses the feature, you block that user, not your whole account. And your instructions to the model and the model choice can change without an app release. Google offers a managed version of this pattern for Gemini: Firebase AI Logic, with App Check to make sure calls come from your real app.

The analogy

A company card. You don't hand the card to every customer and trust them to buy only what you meant. A cashier holds it, checks who's asking, applies the limit, and pays.

Check yourself

The key is in the APK, obfuscated by R8. Is it safe?

Not quite. R8 renames code; the key is still a value the app sends.

Right. If the app can send it, users can read it.

Not quite. HTTPS protects the wire from others, not from the phone's owner.

With a proxy backend, one user floods the AI feature. What can you do?

Right. The server sees users, not only a key.

Not quite. Every request passes your server first, which can refuse it.

Not quite. The key isn't in the app any more; you act on the user instead.

What's the difference between an API key and the user's login token?

Right. Your account vs your user.

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Sources

  • Google Cloud: Best practices for managing API keys ("Don't include API keys in client code or commit them to code repositories. API keys hardcoded in the source code or stored in a repository are open to interception or theft by bad actors. The client should pass requests to the server, which can add the credential and issue the request.")

What you now know

Anything in your APK can be extracted, so an API key in the app belongs to anyone who downloads it, and they can spend your money. Call the model through a proxy backend: the app authenticates the user to your server, and the server adds the key, applies per-user limits and calls the model. The key never leaves the server.
